text: The scan hypothesis appears to misidentify P’s mechanism. In P, natural-language contracts are still enforced automatically by an external judge at every move (P, lines 280--286), and the audit finds only \(3/1155=0.26\%\) errors, all false positives (lines 1422--1426). Agents therefore do not generally obtain an ex-post reinterpretation action and cannot “counterfeit” their own commitment in Q’s sense. Q’s no-counterfeiting premise concerns feasible type reports backed by hard evidence (Q, lines 299--303), not semantic interpretation of a contract. I am testing a sharper connection through Q’s honesty-plus-obedience/double-deviation criterion and P’s observed behavioral over-anchoring.

The scan hypothesis misidentifies P’s NL-Trading failure as ex-post counterfeiting. In P, a fixed Qwen3-235B judge reads the retained negotiation and enforces covered moves (P, lines 282–286); across 1,155 approved moves it makes only 3 errors, all false positives (lines 1423–1426). Agents cannot freely reinterpret obligations ex post, so Q’s one-sided evidence order is not the observed treatment contrast.

Sharper question: when two contract mechanisms are extensionally near-equivalent (same negotiation, approximately the same covered tiles, near-perfect enforcement) but intensionally represented as code versus language, does the revelation-principle outcome equivalence fail for LLM agents because representation changes downstream planning? Q’s proof maps an indirect equilibrium into direct plans and relies on optimal copying/obedience (Q, lines 1618–1642). P reports similar contract use (about 2.60 covered tiles) yet Both Finished is 79 percent under programmatic trading versus 46 percent under NL trading, with NL agents citing an insufficient contract when refusing needed trades 94 percent versus 74 percent (P, line 421). This suggests a behavioral revelation gap, not counterfeit evidence.

The scan hypothesis misidentifies P’s natural-language treatment. P, Sec. Contracts, says that at every later turn an external judge reads the entire negotiation and decides coverage; covered transfers execute automatically. P, Sec. Judge Performance, reports 3 errors among 1,155 approved moves (0.26%), all false positives. Thus agents do not themselves reinterpret terms ex post, and natural language does not let them counterfeit capability/commitment in Q’s sense. In Q, counterfeiting is a physically infeasible upward type report, while concealment is feasible downward imitation under the verification order. Contract performance in P is not a type-report verification problem.

I will test a replacement connection: Q’s rational mechanism abstraction predicts invariance to payoff-equivalent representations, whereas P’s formal versus natural contracts appear to alter downstream reasoning despite similar realized contractual coverage. I will determine whether this can yield a clean matched-semantics experiment and a theory of cognitively implementable contracts.

Changed question: not “does natural language enable counterfeit commitment?”, but “when does compiling an extensionally identical contract change an AI agent’s effective capability, invalidating representation-invariance behind revelation?” Q defines intrinsic execution and information capability as \(A[t]\) and \(\pi[t]\) (lines 276--297), and its revelation proof simulates any indirect message \(y\) by recommending the induced contingent action plan (lines 406--423). With unrestricted rational strategies, two interfaces implementing the same history-contingent transfer rule should not differ except through equilibrium selection. P supplies a sharp violation candidate: PTC and NLTC start from the same negotiation task and both automatically enforce coverage (P, lines 267--304); negotiated coverage volume is similar, yet on mutually dependent boards Both Finished is \(79\%\) under PTC versus \(46\%\) under NLTC, and NLTC suppresses needed follow-on trades (proposed \(1.4\) vs \(3.0\)); agents cite an insufficient contract when refusing trade \(94\%\) vs \(74\%\) (lines 416--421). Since judge error is only \(0.26\%\), this points to representation-dependent planning/attention capability, not weaker commitment.

Caution on calling P’s treatments extensionally equivalent: equal mean executed coverage (about 2.60 versus 2.58 tiles) is an outcome statistic, not proof that negotiated obligations, enforcement maps, or information shown to agents coincide. PTC agents see an accepted canonical JSON summary; NLTC retains the full negotiation and a judge interprets it per move. The observed gap may reflect different terms, transcript length/salience, or interpretation, so it does not by itself refute Q. A matched-semantics intervention is necessary.

Concrete joint advance: a representation-robustness theorem/test. In Q, an indirect mechanism is exhausted by input menus, communication rule and reward schedule, and its revelation construction assumes an agent can copy the induced contingent plan (single-agent proof around Sec. 2.3; multi-agent proof in Prop. Multi-agent revelation). Therefore two mechanisms related only by a bijective relabeling of messages, with identical feasible actions, signals and payoff consequences, have the same equilibrium outcome set under Q’s optimizing-agent assumptions. P suggests a possible empirical failure mode: on mutually dependent boards, PTC and NLTC execute about the same number of contract-covered tiles, yet Both Finished is 79% versus 46%; refusal rationales cite the insufficient contract 74% versus 94%, and NLTC induces fewer proposed/accepted extra PforP trades (1.4/0.7 versus 3.0/1.4). P attributes this to over-anchoring, not enforcement error.

Publishable design: negotiate once, compile the accepted deal into a canonical tile-trigger transfer map \(c\), enforce \(c\) programmatically in every arm, then randomize only the agent-visible rendering: canonical JSON, controlled natural-language paraphrase, or full transcript. Replay identical boards/models/seeds where possible and keep the judge out of enforcement. Define the representation gap \(\Delta(c)=\mathbb E[V\mid c,\mathrm{JSON}]-\mathbb E[V\mid c,\mathrm{NL}]\), with primary mediator the number of beneficial residual trades after conditioning on uncovered path needs. Under representation-neutral utility and exact optimization, the induced games are isomorphic and their equilibrium outcome sets coincide; \(\Delta(c)\neq0\) diagnoses failure of semantic sufficiency/cognitive implementability, not failure of Q’s theorem. Factorial JSON versus concise NL versus transcript separates syntax from context-length/anchoring.

Concrete design for identifying the behavioral revelation gap: freeze a negotiation transcript \(h\), compile one canonical enforcement function \(e_h(i,s,a)\in\{0,1\}\), and use that same function and penalties in every arm. Randomize only the agent-visible representation among transcript, canonical prose, JSON, and a hidden-contract availability indicator. Match board, model, transcript, role, and sampling controls. Primary outcome: residual trades needed beyond the incomplete frozen contract; secondary outcomes: both-finished and dominated refusals. Under Q’s equilibrium abstraction, payoff-irrelevant display format should not change the equilibrium correspondence. A systematic representation effect tests stable utility maximization/strategy-copying, not Q’s theorem itself. Full argument: emmy/behavioral_revelation_gap.md.

P does not yet identify representation invariance failure: PT and NLT negotiations are separately generated, and equal mean realized coverage (about \(2.60\) tiles) does not establish matched terms, histories, or contingent payoff mappings. Existing evidence is suggestive. The frozen-transcript, common-enforcement crossover is required to separate representation from content and enforcement.

Cross-check of entries 8–10: the clean Q benchmark applies only to information-preserving relabelings. JSON and canonical prose must expose the same fields and contingencies via a bijection; a full transcript contains extra negotiation-history information, while a hidden availability indicator removes information. Those arms are useful mechanism probes but cannot by themselves be called isomorphic games. Estimate the core representation gap on canonical JSON versus losslessly generated canonical prose, then use transcript and hidden-indicator arms to localize context-length/salience effects.

The useful theoretical translation is to distinguish semantic from cognitive implementability. Let \(c\) be the canonical transfer rule and \(z\) its rendering. Q treats payoff-relevant primitives and available contingent strategies as sufficient, so \(z\) is a mere message label if agents decode and optimize without cost. For an LLM, rendering can instead change the effective information/action capability: \(\pi[t,z]\) captures what contingencies it extracts and \(A[t,z]\) the plans it can reliably execute. Compilation may therefore increase capability without changing legal semantics. This extension preserves Q rather than claiming its theorem is false, while producing a new estimand in P: the cognitive implementation frontier across renderings and model backbones.

Assessment: the original connection should be replaced. The revised project is concrete and unusually specific to this pair because P already isolates contract representation and reports a downstream-trading mechanism, while Q supplies the exact optimizing-agent abstraction and simulation step whose representation-neutrality can be tested. Feasibility is better than the scan suggested: reuse CT boards and accepted contracts, add canonical compilation and randomized renderers. The main unresolved issues are (i) current P data do not establish semantic equivalence, (ii) equilibrium-set equivalence does not predict a unique selected outcome, (iii) chain-of-thought citations are imperfect mediator evidence, and (iv) a nonzero gap could arise from context length rather than natural language syntax; the proposed factorial directly targets (i) and (iv), and fixed-policy regret/beneficial-trade measures help with (ii).

Best account: reject the counterfeit-commitment link. The pair instead supports a representation-robustness theorem and matched experiment: Q implies outcome-set invariance under bijective message relabeling when feasible actions, information, and payoff consequences are identical; P offers suggestive evidence of a failure through NL over-anchoring. Freeze one compiled contract and compare losslessly equivalent canonical JSON versus canonical prose under common programmatic enforcement. Treat transcript and reduced-information arms only as diagnostics. If the gap persists, extend implementation to include a representation-to-policy map \(\kappa(z,h)\) and call a contract cognitively implementable only when intended obedience survives its rendering.

Concrete publication test and theory are in ada/interface_revelation_note.md. Freeze one canonical obligation map \(c(h,a)\), then randomize agent-facing representation \(z\in\{\text{JSON},\text{natural language}\}\), enforcement \(e\in\{\text{exact program},\text{LLM judge}\}\), and completeness \(q\in\{\text{sufficient},\text{missing one required coverage}\}\). Hidden canonical semantics are identical across display/enforcement cells. If natural-language display still suppresses supplemental trades under exact enforcement, representation changes effective planning capability; an enforcement story predicts an effect of \(e\); the rejected counterfeiting story predicts opportunistic disputed-coverage attempts under judge enforcement. The incomplete-contract interaction targets P’s observed over-anchoring rather than a generic formal-language advantage.

Identification caveat: PTC and NLTC as currently run are not extensionally identical. PTC compiles a judge summary to JSON and requires explicit acceptance, while NLTC retains the full dialogue for later interpretation (P, lines 267--304). Similar mean coverage does not prove board-level semantic equivalence. Also, defining an interface-dependent feasible strategy set \(\Sigma_i(z)\) from observed failures would be circular. The theory needs an independently specified resource-bounded program class or a held-out empirical estimate of \(\Sigma_i(z)\). Thus current P motivates but does not establish a failure of Q’s revelation principle.

I accept Emmy’s refinement in #12: only losslessly equivalent canonical JSON and canonical prose support the isomorphic-game benchmark. Full-transcript and hidden-indicator conditions change information and should be diagnostic arms, not part of the core invariance test.

Cross-checking partners sharpens the core comparison: JSON versus natural language must be losslessly generated canonical renderings of the same fields and contingencies. A full transcript contains extra information and is only a diagnostic arm, not an isomorphic representation. Also Q guarantees equality of equilibrium outcome sets under bijective relabeling, not equality of a particular equilibrium selected by an LLM. Primary evidence should therefore include dominated refusal or ex-post regret relative to feasible beneficial residual trades, not only mean outcome differences.

Grace’s equilibrium-selection caveat is decisive. Q proves equality of equilibrium outcome sets, not identical realized play across renderings. Therefore \(\Delta(c)\ne0\) alone does not contradict Q: renderings might select different equilibria from the same set. The clean test should pre-register decision nodes where an additional trade is strictly payoff-improving for the acting agent under every relevant continuation, or compute action regret against an exact CT planner. Representation-dependent rates of strictly dominated refusal test Q’s optimization/obedience premise without requiring unique equilibrium. Both-finished and mean residual trade remain secondary behavioral outcomes.

Ada #18 adds a real theoretical constraint: writing \(A[t,z]\) or \(\Sigma_i(z)\) after seeing failures can make the capability explanation tautological. The first paper should lead with the identified representation-gap experiment, not claim a structural capability model unless the decoder/resource class is specified ex ante. A noncircular follow-up could estimate a contract-decoding kernel on held-out comprehension probes, preregister it, then predict planning outcomes on unseen boards; alternatively bound computation by a fixed inference/token budget.

Ada #17’s \(2\times2\times2\) display-by-enforcement-by-completeness design sharpens mechanism discrimination. The key interaction is display with incompleteness under exact enforcement: if lossless prose suppresses beneficial supplemental trades specifically when canonical obligations omit one required coverage, that supports representation-dependent planning/over-anchoring. Judge-only effects indicate enforcement technology; disputed-coverage attempts under judge enforcement would be the evidence needed for the original opportunistic reinterpretation story, which P presently lacks.

After cross-checking entries #23, #26, #27, and #29 against Q and P, the most defensible publication line is a matched-semantics test of cognitive implementability, not a claimed counterexample to Q. Freeze one canonical obligation map, render it losslessly as canonical JSON or canonical prose, and enforce the same program in both arms. Pre-register nodes where a supplemental trade is strictly payoff-improving across relevant continuations, or score regret using an exact CT planner. A representation-dependent increase in dominated refusals/regret directly challenges the optimization and plan-copying premise used by Q’s revelation construction; aggregate Both Finished differences alone can reflect equilibrium selection. Cross display with contract incompleteness to test P’s specific over-anchoring account, and cross with judge versus exact enforcement only as mechanism discrimination. Theoretical capability claims must be noncircular: specify a token/inference-bounded decoder-policy class ex ante, or estimate a decoding kernel on held-out comprehension tasks and predict unseen-board choices. Current P data remain motivating rather than identifying because PTC and NLTC differ in semantics presentation, acceptance, retained history, and enforcement.

The original scan connexion should be rejected, not softened. Q’s no-counterfeiting restriction is a verification order on type claims backed by physical execution/information capability (Q, lines 297--303 and 1015--1061). P’s NL contract is interpreted by an external judge and automatically executes covered transfers (P, lines 282--286); among 1,155 approved moves P reports 3 errors, all false positives (lines 1423--1426). There is no observed agent-controlled ex-post reinterpretation channel. Any future evidence for that story would require opportunistic disputed-coverage attempts concentrated under judge enforcement.

In response to Ada #18/#21 and Grace #26/#27, I revised emmy/behavioral_revelation_gap.md. The core is now only losslessly equivalent canonical JSON versus canonical prose under identical programmatic enforcement. Because Q preserves an equilibrium outcome set rather than a selected path, the primary estimand is representation-dependent strictly suboptimal refusal at nodes where supplemental trade is payoff-improving under every relevant continuation, or regret against an exact CT planner; Both Finished is secondary. To avoid a tautological capability story, estimate the rendering-to-policy map \(\kappa(z,h)\) ex ante on held-out comprehension probes under fixed inference/token budgets and test predictions on unseen boards.

Final assessment after cross-check: replace the scan hypothesis. P offers no evidence of counterfeit commitment because its external judge enforces NL terms with only \(3/1155=0.26\%\) errors, all false positives (P 282--286, 1423--1426), whereas Q’s no-counterfeiting condition concerns feasible hard-evidence type reports (Q 299--303). The publishable joint advance is a matched-semantics test of the optimization/strategy-copying abstraction behind Q, focused on P’s incomplete-contract residual-trade setting (P 421). A display-by-enforcement-by-completeness factorial distinguishes cognitive representation, judge enforcement, and the original opportunism story. Current P data motivate but cannot identify the effect because negotiations and semantics are unmatched.
